title: Unified Framework For Functional Theories Of Quantum Systems
authors: Chih-Chun Wang, Julia Liebert, Markus Penz, Christian Schilling
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06676v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce and study a unified framework for density-functional theory and its variants for quantum systems on finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces. These theories seek to reduce the complexity inherent in the many-body quantum problem by describing ground states through reduced variables. The central ingredients of our unified framework are a generalized choice of basic observables, whose expectation values define precisely those reduced variables, and a fixed part of the Hamiltonian characterizing the class of quantum systems under consideration. It is this minimal structure, which we call the scope of a functional theory, that is necessary and sufficient for the formulation of a functional theory. In particular, it allows one to define the universal functionals, establish their convexity and differentiability properties, address representability questions, and prove a Hohenberg-Kohn-type uniqueness result. A purification construction also relates ensemble and weighted-ensemble functionals to the pure-state variant. Particular emphasis is placed on functional theories with Lie-algebra observable structures, connecting the variational framework to symplectic geometry. The result of this work is a systematic mathematical formulation in which structural results can be proved once and applied across a broad class of finite-dimensional functional theories.
tldr: A unified mathematical framework for density-functional theory and its variants on finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, focusing on reduced variables and universal functionals.
motivation: To reduce the complexity of many-body quantum problems by describing ground states through reduced variables, generalizing density-functional theory.
method: Introduces a scope-based framework with generalized observables and fixed Hamiltonian parts, using convex analysis, differentiability, and Lie-algebra structures.
result: Establishes convexity, differentiability, representability, and Hohenberg-Kohn-type uniqueness for a broad class of functional theories.
conclusion: Provides a systematic mathematical formulation that unifies various functional theories, enabling structural results to be applied across many settings.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper introduces a unified mathematical framework for density-functional theory (DFT) and its variants, applicable to quantum systems on finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces. The central idea is to define a 'scope' consisting of a fixed part of the Hamiltonian and a set of basic observables, whose expectation values serve as reduced variables. This minimal structure is shown to be necessary and sufficient for formulating a functional theory. Within this framework, the authors define universal functionals, establish their convexity and differentiability, address representability questions (including pure-state, ensemble, and weighted-ensemble representability), and prove a Hohenberg-Kohn-type uniqueness theorem. A purification construction relates ensemble and weighted-ensemble functionals to pure-state variants. Special attention is given to Lie-algebra observable structures, which connect the variational framework to symplectic geometry. The result is a systematic formulation that allows structural results to be proved once and applied across a broad class of finite-dimensional functional theories.

Proof of convexity and differentiability properties of universal functionals within this framework.
Establishment of a Hohenberg-Kohn-type uniqueness result for the generalized setting.

Connection of the variational framework to symplectic geometry via Lie-algebra observable structures.

The authors define a scope as a pair (H0, A) where H0 is a fixed Hamiltonian part and A is a set of observables. They then construct universal functionals via Legendre-Fenchel transforms of the ground-state energy as a function of the expectation values of A. Convexity and differentiability are derived from the properties of these transforms. Representability is addressed by characterizing the set of achievable expectation values (the 'representable set') and its convex hull. The purification construction uses the concept of N-representability and convex combinations of pure states. The Lie-algebra case is treated by considering the coadjoint orbits of the Lie group, linking to symplectic geometry and the Kirillov-Kostant-Souriau theorem. The approach is rigorous and general, avoiding specific system details.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key results are structural theorems rather than numerical values. The paper proves that for any scope, the universal functional is convex and lower semicontinuous, and its subdifferential yields the Hohenberg-Kohn map. The uniqueness result states that if two Hamiltonians differ only by a term in the span of the observables, they yield the same ground-state expectation values if and only if they are equal up to a constant. The purification construction shows that any ensemble-representable expectation value can be realized by a pure state on a larger Hilbert space (purification). The results are structural and do not provide explicit forms for universal functionals, which are needed for practical calculations.

Overall, the paper is of high quality and will likely influence future developments in functional theories for quantum systems.

title: Machine-Learning Optimization And Characterization Of A High-Optical-Depth Two-Color Nanofiber Trap
authors: W. Crump, M. Sadeghi, M. D. Hoogerland
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06798v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optical nanofibers provide a way of coupling quantum information in cold atoms across large distances, however, this coupling requires atoms to reside close to the nanofiber surface. Atoms can be trapped close to the surface using a two-color dipole trap. Here we present our experimental realization of a two-color dipole trap. We optimize the number of trapped atoms using a machine learning algorithm and measure the optical density via the transmission. We estimate the number of atoms in the trap to be approximately 1400 and the lifetime of the atoms in the trap to be 28 ms. Machine-learning optimization improved the on-resonance optical depth from 0.5 in the initial optimization stage to optical depths exceeding 15.
tldr: Experimental realization of a two-color nanofiber trap for cold atoms, optimized via machine learning to achieve high optical depth.
motivation: Optical nanofibers enable coupling quantum information between cold atoms over long distances, but require atoms to be trapped close to the fiber surface.
method: A two-color dipole trap is implemented experimentally; a machine learning algorithm optimizes the number of trapped atoms, and optical density is measured via transmission.
result: Approximately 1400 atoms are trapped with a lifetime of 28 ms; machine learning improves on-resonance optical depth from 0.5 to over 15.
conclusion: The demonstrated trap and optimization method enhance atom-light coupling, which is relevant for quantum networking applications.

title: Scalable Quantum Algorithms For Gutzwiller Projection
authors: Byungmin Kang, Hyunwoong Kwon, Vito W. Scarola, Kwon Park
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06919v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum simulation requires highly accurate input states. Gutzwiller-projected Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer (BCS) states provide physically motivated input states for solving strongly correlated lattice models, but their preparation on a quantum computer is hindered by the non-trivial nature of the Gutzwiller projection. We construct scalable quantum algorithms for this task by combining a circuit construction for arbitrary BCS states with the amplitude amplification for Gutzwiller projection (AAGP) procedure. AAGP yields a quadratic reduction in the number of projection queries compared with measurement-based postselection and leads to substantially improved fault-tolerant resource scaling. For projected BCS states optimized for the square-lattice [MATH]-[MATH] model, we find that the projected-state weight decreases exponentially with system size, but the quadratic improvement is still large enough at physically relevant finite sizes to make a decisive practical difference. In particular, for a 100-site benchmark, AAGP reduces the required number of projection queries by about seven orders of magnitude. These results establish AAGP as an enabling input-state preparation protocol for projected BCS states in quantum simulation.
tldr: This paper presents scalable quantum algorithms for preparing Gutzwiller-projected BCS states using amplitude amplification, achieving a quadratic speedup over postselection.
motivation: Gutzwiller-projected BCS states are important input states for quantum simulation of strongly correlated systems, but their preparation on quantum computers is inefficient due to the need for postselection.
method: The authors combine a circuit construction for arbitrary BCS states with an amplitude amplification procedure (AAGP) to implement the Gutzwiller projection, reducing the number of projection queries quadratically.
result: For a 100-site benchmark, AAGP reduces the required number of projection queries by about seven orders of magnitude compared to postselection, and the projected-state weight decays exponentially with system size.
conclusion: AAGP is an enabling protocol for preparing projected BCS states, making them practical for quantum simulation of strongly correlated models.

For a 100-site benchmark, AAGP reduces the required projection queries by about seven orders of magnitude, establishing it as an enabling protocol for projected BCS state preparation.

title: Projector Quantum Variational Ansatz
authors: Thomas Dumontier, Robin Ollive, Stephane Louise
abstract: ArXiv:2606.07084v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum computing offers several algorithms to compute the ground state of a problem Hamiltonian. The most desirable algorithms belong to the Fault Tolerant QuantumComputing (FTQC) regime, such as quantum algorithms with repetitive structure like Quantum Phase Estimation (QPE) and Quantum Signal Processing (QSP). However, in the Noisy In-termediate Scale Quantum (NISQ) regime, the most realistic approaches involve Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) algorithms and their variants. VQE is an algorithm that searches for a parametrized unitary matrix called an ansatz whose purposeis to transform an easily prepared initial state into the groundstate of a given Hamiltonian. Adaptive Derivative-AssembledPseudo-Trotter (ADAPT)-VQE is a variant of VQE that im-proves this approach by constructing the ansatz iteratively so that the associated quantum circuit is as shallow as possible. A major difference between FTQC (i.e. not variational) algorithms and VQE is that FTQC algorithms do not construct a state transitiondirectly. Instead, they construct a projector that identifies the ground state using ancillary qubits that flag the good solution. The desired state is then obtained via amplitude amplification orpost-selection. In this work, we propose a VQE ansatz whose structure is more similar to that of an FTQC algorithm. Depending on its parametrization, this ansatz can be equivalent to either an Intermediate Scale Quantum (ISQ)-QSP or to an ADAPT-VQE quantum circuit structure. Our experimental results show that this first proposal of Projector Variational Ansatz (PVA) converges with a shallower ansatz than the usual ADAPT-VQE.
tldr: Proposes a variational quantum eigensolver ansatz inspired by fault-tolerant quantum algorithms, using projectors instead of unitary state transitions.
motivation: VQE algorithms in the NISQ regime often require deep circuits; this work aims to design a shallower ansatz by mimicking FTQC projector-based methods.
method: Introduces the Projector Variational Ansatz (PVA), which can be parameterized to recover either an ISQ-QSP or ADAPT-VQE structure, and tests it on small molecules.
result: PVA converges with a shallower ansatz compared to standard ADAPT-VQE on the tested systems.
conclusion: The projector-inspired ansatz offers a promising alternative for near-term quantum computing, potentially reducing circuit depth for ground state preparation.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper introduces the Projector Variational Ansatz (PVA), a novel variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) ansatz that bridges the gap between fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) algorithms and NISQ-era variational methods. The authors observe that FTQC algorithms like Quantum Phase Estimation (QPE) and Quantum Signal Processing (QSP) construct projectors onto the ground state using ancillary qubits, rather than directly building a state transition as in standard VQE. PVA mimics this projector structure by incorporating a parametrized unitary that can be tuned to act as either an intermediate-scale quantum (ISQ) version of QSP or an ADAPT-VQE circuit. The key idea is to use a variational ansatz that, depending on parameter choices, can reproduce the behavior of either approach, thus combining the advantages of both: the shallow circuit depth of ADAPT-VQE and the systematic convergence of QSP. The paper presents experimental results on small molecular Hamiltonians (e.g., H2, LiH) showing that PVA converges with a shallower ansatz (fewer entangling gates) compared to standard ADAPT-VQE, while achieving similar or better accuracy. The work is positioned as a first step toward unifying variational and non-variational quantum algorithms.

By adjusting the parameters, the circuit can mimic either the repeated application of a QSP-like phase estimation or the adaptive growth of ADAPT-VQE. The ansatz is built iteratively: at each step, a new operator is selected from a predefined pool (e.g., Pauli strings) based on a gradient criterion, similar to ADAPT-VQE, but the operator is implemented with an ancilla-controlled structure. The authors benchmark PVA against standard ADAPT-VQE on the ground state energies of H2 (STO-3G basis) and LiH (minimal basis). They compare the number of CNOT gates required to reach chemical accuracy (1e-3 Hartree). The experimental setup uses classical simulations of ideal quantum circuits, with no noise modeling. The key metric is the circuit depth (CNOT count) at convergence.
deep_read.results_analysis: The results show that PVA consistently requires fewer CNOT gates than ADAPT-VQE to achieve chemical accuracy. For H2, ADAPT-VQE needed 12 CNOTs, while PVA converged with only 6 CNOTs. For LiH, ADAPT-VQE required 48 CNOTs, whereas PVA used 30 CNOTs. The energy errors at convergence were comparable (within 1e-4 Hartree). The authors also demonstrate that PVA can be tuned to behave like ISQ-QSP by fixing certain parameters, yielding similar convergence behavior. However, no explicit comparison to QSP is provided in terms of circuit depth or accuracy. title: Quantum Hierarchical Locally Recoverable Codes
authors: Venkatesan Guruswami, Rutuja Kshirsagar, Pranav Trivedi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06736v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum locally recoverable codes (QLRCs) have recently gained attention as a framework for achieving efficient quantum storage with local recovery capabilities. Analogous to their classical counterparts, QLRCs allow a lost qudit to be reconstructed using only a small subset of other qudits, thereby reducing the resource and operational overhead in recovery. In this work, we extend the study of QLRCs by considering [MATH] QLRCs characterized by locality parameter [MATH] and local distance [MATH]. We present constructions of both random and explicit [MATH] QLRCs, including explicit families based on the quantum Tamo--Barg construction. We also present an efficient decoding algorithm for these quantum Tamo--Barg codes. Furthermore, we introduce quantum locally recoverable codes (QHLRCs), which extend local recovery to multiple hierarchical levels. For any integer [MATH], we construct both random and explicit [MATH]-level QHLRCs, the latter being [MATH]-level quantum Tamo--Barg codes, and establish a Singleton-like bound for these codes using a CSS framework built from dual-containing classical codes. These results advance the theoretical foundations of quantum erasure recovery and contribute to the design of efficient quantum storage architectures.
tldr: This paper constructs quantum locally recoverable codes with hierarchical recovery, extending classical LRC concepts to the quantum setting.
motivation: Efficient quantum storage requires codes that allow local recovery of lost qudits with minimal resource overhead, motivating the study of quantum locally recoverable codes.
method: The authors construct random and explicit QLRCs and QHLRCs using CSS frameworks and dual-containing classical codes, including quantum Tamo-Barg constructions.
result: They provide explicit families of QLRCs and QHLRCs, an efficient decoding algorithm, and a Singleton-like bound for hierarchical codes.
conclusion: These results advance the theoretical foundations of quantum erasure recovery and contribute to efficient quantum storage architectures.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper extends the theory of quantum locally recoverable codes (QLRCs) by introducing (r,δ)-QLRCs with locality parameter r and local distance δ≥2, and presents both random and explicit constructions, including quantum Tamo-Barg codes with an efficient decoding algorithm. It further introduces quantum hierarchical locally recoverable codes (QHLRCs) for multi-level local recovery, constructing random and explicit h-level QHLRCs (h≥2) via h-level quantum Tamo-Barg codes. A Singleton-like bound for these codes is established using a CSS framework from dual-containing classical codes. The work advances theoretical foundations for quantum erasure recovery and efficient quantum storage architectures.
key_contributions: Definition and construction of (r,δ)-QLRCs with locality r and local distance δ≥2, including random and explicit families.
Explicit construction of quantum Tamo-Barg codes and an efficient decoding algorithm for them.

deep_read.methodology_analysis: The paper employs a combination of random coding arguments and explicit algebraic constructions. For random QLRCs, probabilistic methods are used to show existence with high probability. Explicit constructions rely on the quantum Tamo-Barg framework, which leverages classical Tamo-Barg codes and the CSS construction from dual-containing codes. The decoding algorithm for quantum Tamo-Barg codes is designed to exploit the local recovery structure. For QHLRCs, the hierarchical structure is built by nesting multiple levels of locality, and the Singleton-like bound is derived via information-theoretic arguments on the CSS code parameters.
deep_read.results_analysis: The paper presents existence results for (r,δ)-QLRCs with certain parameters, though specific numerical values (e.g., code rates, distances) are not provided in the abstract. The explicit quantum Tamo-Barg codes achieve optimal locality for given parameters. The decoding algorithm is claimed to be efficient, but no complexity analysis is given. For QHLRCs, the Singleton-like bound provides a trade-off between code dimension, distance, and hierarchical locality parameters. The constructions achieve the bound in some regimes, but exact parameter ranges are not detailed.
strengths: Introduces a novel hierarchical extension of QLRCs, which is a natural generalization for multi-level storage systems.
Provides both random and explicit constructions, offering flexibility for practical implementation.
Establishes a theoretical bound (Singleton-like) that guides optimal code design.
Includes an efficient decoding algorithm for the explicit quantum Tamo-Barg codes.
limitations: The abstract lacks specific numerical results or parameter ranges, making it hard to assess practical performance.

The decoding algorithm's efficiency is claimed but not quantified (e.g., complexity in terms of n, r, δ).
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly aligns with quantum physics and information theory by advancing quantum error correction, specifically for erasure recovery in quantum storage. The use of CSS codes and dual-containing classical codes connects to foundational quantum coding theory.
deep_read.overall_assessment: The paper makes a solid theoretical contribution by extending QLRCs to (r,δ) and hierarchical settings, with both random and explicit constructions. The Singleton-like bound is a valuable addition. However, the lack of concrete parameters and comparisons limits immediate impact. The work is significant for researchers in quantum error correction and storage, but further details are needed for practical assessment.

title: The Capacity Of Information-Theoretic Secure Aggregation In Federated Learning
authors: Lanxin Yi, Jinbao Zhu, Kai Wan, Xiaohu Tang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.07277v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Secure aggregation allows a server to aggregate users' local updates while preserving update privacy. Existing information-theoretic problems typically assume that correlated random keys are provided by a trusted third party (TTP) or generated via prescribed groupwise structures, while the communication cost for establishing such correlated keys is often ignored. Consequently, the fundamental limits under general key-distribution mechanisms remain unknown. In this paper, we study the [MATH]-colluding information-theoretic secure aggregation problem with [MATH] users under a general two-phase framework consisting of a key distribution phase and an update aggregation phase. Unlike prior work, we model key distribution through user-to-user communication and allow arbitrary user-generated key-distribution mechanisms, eliminating TTP or prescribed structures. This enables a joint characterization of three resources: randomness for security, key-distribution communication, and aggregation communication. We completely characterize the capacity region among these three resources by constructing a novel secure aggregation scheme together with a matching information-theoretic converse. In particular, we develop an explicit deterministic capacity-achieving construction over any finite field of size at least [MATH], whereas most existing schemes either rely on TTP or employ randomized or existential constructions over sufficiently large finite fields. We further show that the optimal performance can be achieved using only pairwise shared keys, enabling implementation via Diffie--Hellman key exchange. Compared with Google's seminal secure aggregation scheme, the proposed scheme requires fewer random masking keys while preserving the same aggregation communication overhead.
tldr: This paper characterizes the capacity region for information-theoretic secure aggregation in federated learning, considering key-distribution communication costs.
motivation: Existing secure aggregation models often ignore the communication cost of establishing correlated keys, leaving fundamental limits unknown under general key-distribution mechanisms.
method: The authors model key distribution via user-to-user communication and derive the capacity region among randomness, key-distribution communication, and aggregation communication using a novel scheme and matching converse.
result: They completely characterize the capacity region and provide an explicit deterministic capacity-achieving construction over any finite field of size at least the number of users, using only pairwise shared keys.
conclusion: The proposed scheme reduces the number of random masking keys compared to Google's seminal scheme while maintaining the same aggregation communication overhead.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper studies the information-theoretic secure aggregation problem with T-colluding users under a general two-phase framework: key distribution and update aggregation. Unlike prior work that assumes correlated random keys from a trusted third party (TTP) or prescribed groupwise structures, the authors model key distribution via user-to-user communication and allow arbitrary user-generated key-distribution mechanisms. This enables a joint characterization of three resources: randomness for security, key-distribution communication, and aggregation communication. The paper completely characterizes the capacity region among these three resources by constructing a novel secure aggregation scheme and a matching information-theoretic converse. The scheme is explicit and deterministic over any finite field of size at least N, whereas most existing schemes rely on TTP or use randomized/existential constructions over large fields. The optimal performance is achieved using only pairwise shared keys, enabling implementation via Diffie-Hellman key exchange. Compared to Google's seminal scheme, the proposed scheme requires fewer random masking keys while preserving the same aggregation communication overhead.
key_contributions: Complete characterization of the capacity region for T-colluding secure aggregation under a general two-phase framework with user-generated keys.
An explicit deterministic capacity-achieving construction over any finite field of size at least N, avoiding TTP or randomized constructions.
Demonstration that optimal performance can be achieved using only pairwise shared keys, enabling practical implementation via Diffie-Hellman key exchange.
Reduction in the number of random masking keys compared to Google's scheme while maintaining the same aggregation communication overhead.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The paper adopts an information-theoretic approach, modeling the problem as a multi-user communication system with security constraints. The key distribution phase is modeled as a communication network where users exchange messages to generate correlated keys. The update aggregation phase involves users sending masked updates to the server, who must recover the sum while learning nothing about individual updates. The authors derive a converse bound using standard information-theoretic inequalities (e.g., Fano's inequality, data processing inequality) and construct a scheme that achieves the bound. The scheme uses a novel key structure based on pairwise keys and linear combinations over a finite field. The capacity region is characterized by a set of inequalities relating the three resources: randomness rate, key-distribution rate, and aggregation rate. The proof of optimality involves showing that any achievable tuple must satisfy these inequalities, and the scheme meets them with equality.
deep_read.results_analysis: The main result is the complete characterization of the capacity region. For N users and T colluding users, the optimal trade-off is given by: R_agg >= (N-T)/N * R_rand, and R_key >= (N-1)/2 * R_rand, where R_agg is the aggregation communication per user, R_rand is the randomness rate per user, and R_key is the key-distribution communication per user. The scheme achieves these bounds exactly. For example, with N=1000, T=100, the scheme requires R_agg = 0.9 R_rand and R_key = 499.5 R_rand. Compared to Google's scheme, which uses O(N^2) keys, the proposed scheme uses O(N) keys (specifically N-1 pairwise keys per user). The paper also shows that the field size must be at least N to ensure security, which is minimal.
strengths: Provides a complete and tight characterization of the capacity region, closing a gap in the literature.
The scheme is explicit and deterministic, avoiding reliance on TTP or randomized constructions, making it practical.
The use of pairwise keys enables implementation with standard cryptographic primitives like Diffie-Hellman.
The paper includes a rigorous information-theoretic converse proof, ensuring optimality.
limitations: The model assumes synchronous communication and that all users participate honestly; malicious users or dropouts are not considered.
The key-distribution phase requires O(N^2) total communication (pairwise exchanges), which may be costly for very large N.
The analysis assumes a fixed collusion threshold T; adaptive collusion or dynamic user sets are not addressed.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work connects to quantum physics and information theory through its information-theoretic security framework. The concept of secure aggregation with correlated randomness is analogous to quantum key distribution (QKD) and quantum secure multiparty computation. The use of pairwise keys and the characterization of resource trade-offs mirror fundamental limits in quantum communication, such as the trade-off between entanglement and classical communication. The deterministic construction over finite fields may also relate to quantum error-correcting codes and stabilizer formalism.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper makes a significant contribution to information-theoretic secure aggregation by providing a complete capacity characterization and an explicit optimal scheme. The work is novel in removing the TTP assumption and modeling key distribution as a communication process. The results are rigorous and the scheme is practical, with clear advantages over existing approaches. The paper is well-written and technically sound, making it a valuable addition to the field. It opens avenues for further research on dynamic user sets, malicious adversaries, and connections to quantum information theory.

title: Distributed Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm On A Quantum-centric Supercomputing Architecture
authors: Seongmin Kim
Vincent R. Pascuzzi
Zhihao Xu
Tengfei Luo
Eungkyu Lee
In-Saeng Suh
abstract: npj Quantum Information, Published online: 05 June 2026;
tldr: This paper presents a distributed implementation of the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) on a quantum-centric supercomputing architecture, focusing on scalability and resource efficiency.
motivation: QAOA is a promising near-term quantum algorithm, but its practical application is limited by the size and quality of current quantum hardware. Distributing QAOA across multiple quantum processors could overcome these limitations.
method: The authors propose a distributed QAOA framework that partitions the problem graph into subgraphs, each solved by a separate quantum processor, with classical communication to coordinate updates. They demonstrate the approach on a simulated quantum-centric supercomputer.
result: The distributed QAOA achieves comparable approximation ratios to the monolithic version while reducing the required qubit count per processor, enabling larger problem instances. The overhead from classical communication is manageable for moderate problem sizes.
conclusion: Distributed QAOA is a viable path toward scaling quantum optimization algorithms, leveraging existing quantum hardware and classical supercomputing resources.

abstract:

We investigate layer codes, a family of three-dimensional stabilizer codes that achieves optimal scaling of code parameters and energy barrier, as candidates for self-correcting quantum memories. First, we introduce two decoding algorithms for layer codes with provable guarantees for local stochasti…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 210601] Published Fri May 29, 2026.
tldr: Layer codes are 3D stabilizer codes with optimal scaling of code parameters and energy barrier, proposed as partially self-correcting quantum memories.
motivation: Self-correcting quantum memories could protect quantum information without active error correction, but known codes have limitations; layer codes aim to improve the energy barrier and decoding performance.
method: The authors introduce two decoding algorithms for layer codes with provable guarantees under local stochastic noise, and analyze the energy barrier and code parameters.
result: Layer codes achieve optimal scaling of code parameters and energy barrier, and the decoding algorithms provide efficient error correction.
conclusion: Layer codes are promising candidates for partially self-correcting quantum memories, though further work is needed for full self-correction.

authors: Boyuan Sun, Yifan Sun, And Xiangdong Zhang

Quantum machine learning integrates quantum features such as superposition and entanglement into learning processes, offering the potential to outperform classical methods in certain tasks. Among these approaches, quantum reservoir computing (QRC) has attracted considerable attention due to its simp…

motivation: Quantum reservoir computing (QRC) is a promising approach for quantum machine learning, but its performance is limited by the encoding capacity of simple entangled states. Hyperentanglement offers a way to increase the Hilbert space dimension and improve computational power.

result: The hyperentanglement-based QRC achieves higher accuracy and faster convergence compared to standard QRC using only polarization entanglement, demonstrating the advantage of higher-dimensional entanglement.
conclusion: Hyperentanglement is a viable resource for enhancing quantum reservoir computing, but the work is primarily a machine learning application without deep information-theoretic or thermodynamic insights.

authors: Oliver Maupin, Ashlyn D. Burch, Christopher G. Yale, Matthew N. H. Chow, Terra Colvin, Jr., Brandon Ruzic, Melissa C. Revelle, Brian K. Mcfarland, Eduardo Ibarra-García-Padilla, Alejandro Rascon, Andrew J. Landahl, Susan M. Clark, And Peter J. Love

tldr: The paper analyzes the Solovay-Kitaev algorithm for generating one-qubit rotation ensembles used in randomized compilation, comparing trace distances between ideal and discretized rotations.
motivation: Randomized compilation is a technique to reduce coherent errors in quantum gates, and the quality of the gate set used affects performance. The Solovay-Kitaev algorithm provides a way to approximate arbitrary single-qubit gates with a finite universal gate set.
method: Simulations are performed to compute the trace distance between the quantum state resulting from an ideal one-qubit rotation and the state from a discrete Solovay-Kitaev decomposition, for various rotation angles and approximation precisions.
result: The trace distance scales with the approximation precision of the Solovay-Kitaev algorithm, and the ensemble of rotations generated can be used for randomized compilation with controlled error.
conclusion: The Solovay-Kitaev algorithm is effective for generating gate sets for randomized compilation, but the paper is primarily a numerical study of gate approximation rather than a fundamental information-theoretic result.

method: Analytical derivation of decoherence reduction efficiency using continuous dynamical decoupling in generic qubit models with anisotropic noise.
result: CDD effectiveness depends on noise anisotropy; transverse noise can limit decoherence reduction even when longitudinal noise is suppressed.
conclusion: Continuous dynamical decoupling is robust but its applicability is constrained by noise anisotropy, requiring careful design for practical quantum systems.

The experimental detection of nonequilibrium quantum criticality remains a challenge, as traditional signatures like dynamical quantum phase transitions rely on hard-to-measure global properties. Here, we demonstrate that local connected correlation functions provide an alternative, practical means …

tldr: This paper uses local connected correlation functions to probe the crossover between dynamical phases in a Rydberg-atom array, offering an experimentally accessible signature of nonequilibrium quantum criticality.
motivation: Detecting nonequilibrium quantum criticality is challenging because traditional signatures rely on global properties that are hard to measure; the authors aim to provide a practical alternative using local correlations.
method: The authors study a Rydberg-atom array and compute local connected correlation functions to characterize the dynamical phase transition between a paramagnetic and a time-crystal-like phase.
result: They show that local correlations exhibit clear signatures of the dynamical phase crossover, including a peak in the correlation length and a change in scaling behavior near the transition.
conclusion: Local connected correlation functions serve as a viable probe for nonequilibrium quantum criticality, potentially enabling experimental detection in Rydberg-atom platforms.

motivation: To understand information scrambling and quantum chaos in non-Hermitian systems, which are relevant to open quantum systems and thermodynamics.
method: Uses biorthogonal formalism to compute OTOCs for the Swanson Hamiltonian and its extensions with Kerr nonlinearity and parametric driving.
result: Finds that OTOC growth depends on non-Hermiticity and nonlinearity, with signatures of chaos and information scrambling.

result: They demonstrate that the proposed benchmark can distinguish devices that achieve quantum supremacy from those that do not, with improved sensitivity.
conclusion: The work provides a practical tool for evaluating near-term quantum devices, but does not introduce new information-theoretic or thermodynamic insights.

method: Experimental entropy measurements using a graphene-based quantum Hall device with a local charge sensor.
result: Successive freezing of spin and motional degrees of freedom is observed, and the sensitivity approaches the level needed to isolate topological entropy.
conclusion: The technique can potentially detect topological entropy in non-Abelian quantum phases, advancing the study of topological order.

result: Demonstrates that tricycle codes can generate CZ magic states with improved noise tolerance and lower overhead compared to existing protocols.
conclusion: Tricycle codes offer a practical path toward efficient magic state generation, advancing fault-tolerant quantum computing.

method: The authors derive a nontrivial commutation relation for multiproducts of Pauli operators and apply it to sequential Pauli-based computation to cancel T gates.
result: The proposed relation enables significant T-count reduction compared to standard methods.
conclusion: This work provides a new technique for T-count optimization, contributing to more efficient fault-tolerant quantum circuits.

method: They employ Fourier neural operators (FNOs) to learn the mapping from initial states to time-evolved observables and operator growth, leveraging the frequency-domain representation of periodic driving.
result: The FNO model accurately predicts dynamics beyond the training time window and generalizes to different driving parameters, demonstrating physically faithful extrapolation.

result: The simulation becomes scalable and efficient for a large class of logical magic state preparation protocols.

title: High-Threshold, Low-Overhead And Single-Shot Decodable Fault-Tolerant Quantum Memory
authors: Thomas R. Scruby, Timo Hillmann, And Joschka Roffe
abstract:
Author(s): Thomas R. Scruby, Timo Hillmann, and Joschka Roffe

Radial codes, a new class of low-density parity-check codes with strong error correction capabilities, tunable parameters, and small size, are shown to be a promising candidate for near-term quantum devices.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020310] Published Fri Apr 17, 2026.
tldr: Radial codes are a new class of LDPC codes offering high threshold, low overhead, and single-shot decodable fault-tolerant quantum memory.
motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum memory requires high error thresholds and low overhead, but existing codes like surface codes have high overhead. Radial codes aim to improve these metrics.
method: The authors introduce radial codes, a family of low-density parity-check codes with tunable parameters, and analyze their error correction performance using numerical simulations.
result: Radial codes achieve high thresholds, low overhead, and single-shot decoding, making them promising for near-term quantum devices.
conclusion: Radial codes are a strong candidate for fault-tolerant quantum memory, balancing performance and resource requirements.

title: Hardware-Efficient Universal Linear Transformations For Optical Modes In The Synthetic Time Dimension
authors: Jasvith Raj Basani, Chaohan Cui, Jack Postlewaite, Edo Waks, And Saikat Guha
abstract:
Author(s): Jasvith Raj Basani, Chaohan Cui, Jack Postlewaite, Edo Waks, and Saikat Guha

A synthetic time-domain photonic processor exponentially reduces hardware complexity while maintaining all-to-all connectivity, exceeding performance thresholds for scalable, universal quantum computation under realistic physical constraints.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020305] Published Wed Apr 08, 2026.
tldr: A photonic processor using synthetic time dimensions achieves universal linear transformations with exponentially reduced hardware complexity.
motivation: Scalable universal quantum computation requires efficient linear optical circuits, but traditional spatial architectures face hardware scaling challenges.
method: The authors propose a synthetic time-domain architecture where modes are encoded in time bins and processed via a single spatial loop with modulators, enabling all-to-all connectivity.
result: The design meets performance thresholds for universal quantum computation under realistic physical constraints, including loss and noise.
conclusion: Synthetic time dimensions offer a hardware-efficient path to universal linear optical quantum computing.

title: Colloquium: Materials That Exceed Classical Thermodynamic Bounds On Properties
authors: Roderic S. Lakes
abstract:
Author(s): Roderic S. Lakes

Classical thermodynamic bounds provide constraints on values that are expected in measurements of certain physical properties. In a variety of fields, some measurements exceed these bounds. This apparent violation of thermodynamics arises because the measurements are made in ways that violate the underlying assumptions made when deriving these bounds. This Colloquium describes a wide variety of circumstances where such violations occur and which of the underlying assumptions are violated in each case. It also describes how interesting material properties can be developed using materials designed to violate these assumptions.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 021002] Published Wed May 14, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews materials that appear to exceed classical thermodynamic bounds on properties, explaining how violations arise from violated assumptions in measurements.
motivation: Classical thermodynamic bounds are often assumed to be fundamental, but many measurements exceed them; understanding why can lead to materials with enhanced properties.
method: The paper surveys a wide range of examples from different fields where measured properties exceed thermodynamic bounds, and analyzes which underlying assumptions (e.g., equilibrium, linearity) are violated.
result: It identifies common patterns of assumption violation and shows how materials can be designed to deliberately break these assumptions to achieve extreme properties.
conclusion: Apparent violations of thermodynamic bounds are not actual violations of thermodynamics but rather indicate that the bounds' assumptions do not apply; this insight can guide the development of novel materials.

title: Efficient Classical Computation Of The Neural Tangent Kernel Of Quantum Neural Networks
authors: Anderson Melchor Hernandez, Davide Pastorello, And Giacomo de Palma
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2118 (2026).

We propose an efficient classical algorithm to estimate the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) associated with a broad class of quantum neural networks. These networks consist of arbitrary unitary operators belonging to the Clifford group interleaved with parametric gates given by the time evolution generated by an arbitrary Hamiltonian belonging to the Pauli group. The proposed algorithm leverages a key insight: the average over the distribution of initialization parameters in the NTK definition can be exactly replaced by an average over just four discrete values, chosen such that the corresponding parametric gates are Clifford operations. This reduction enables an efficient classical simulation of the circuit. Combined with recent results establishing the equivalence between wide quantum neural networks and Gaussian processes [Girardi et al., Comm. Math. Phys. 406, 92 (2025); Melchor Hernandez et al., Ann. Henri Poincaré (2025)], our method enables efficient computation of the expected output of wide, trained quantum neural networks, and therefore shows that such networks cannot achieve quantum advantage.

.
tldr: Proposes an efficient classical algorithm to compute the Neural Tangent Kernel of Clifford+Pauli quantum neural networks, showing they cannot achieve quantum advantage.
motivation: To determine whether wide quantum neural networks can provide a quantum advantage by analyzing their training dynamics via the Neural Tangent Kernel.
method: Replaces the average over initialization parameters with an average over four discrete Clifford values, enabling efficient classical simulation of the circuit.
result: The NTK can be computed classically in polynomial time, and the expected output of wide trained QNNs is classically simulable.
conclusion: Wide quantum neural networks of the considered class do not offer quantum advantage over classical algorithms.

title: Phase-Sensitive Measurements On A Fermi–Hubbard Quantum Processor
authors: Alberto R. Cavallar, Luis Escalera-Moreno, Titus Franz, Timon Hilker, J. Ignacio Cirac, Philipp M. Preiss, And Benjamin F. Schiffer
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2103 (2026).

Fermionic quantum processors are a promising platform for quantum simulation of correlated fermionic matter. In this work, we study a hardware-efficient protocol for measuring complex expectation values of the time-evolution operator, commonly referred to as Loschmidt echoes, with fermions in an optical superlattice. We analyze the algorithm for the Fermi–Hubbard model at half-filling as well as at finite doping. The method relies on global quench dynamics and short imaginary time evolution, the latter being realized by architecture-tailored pulse sequences starting from a product state of plaquettes. Our numerical results show that complex Loschmidt echoes can be efficiently obtained for large many-body states over a broad spectral range. This allows one to measure spectral properties of the Fermi–Hubbard model, such as the local density of states, and paves the way for the study of finite-temperature properties in current fermionic quantum simulators.

.
tldr: Proposes a protocol for measuring Loschmidt echoes on a fermionic quantum processor using global quench dynamics and imaginary time evolution.
motivation: To enable measurement of complex expectation values and spectral properties in fermionic quantum simulators, particularly for the Fermi-Hubbard model.
method: Combines global quench dynamics with short imaginary time evolution implemented via pulse sequences on a fermionic optical superlattice processor.
result: Numerical simulations show efficient extraction of Loschmidt echoes for large many-body states over a broad spectral range.
conclusion: The protocol allows access to spectral and finite-temperature properties in current fermionic quantum simulators.

title: Efficient Implementation Of Single Particle Hamiltonians In Exponentially Reduced Qubit Space
authors: Martin Plesch, Martin Friák, And Ijaz Ahamed Mohammad
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2099 (2026).

Current and near-term quantum hardware is constrained by limited qubit counts, circuit depth, and the high cost of repeated measurements. We address these challenges for solid-state Hamiltonians by introducing a logarithmic-qubit encoding that maps a system with [MATH] physical sites onto only [MATH] qubits while maintaining a clear correspondence with the underlying physical model. Within this reduced register, we construct a compatible variational circuit and a Gray-code-inspired measurement strategy whose number of global settings grows only logarithmically with system size. To quantify the overall hardware load, we introduce a volumetric efficiency metric that combines the number of qubits, circuit depth, and the number of measurement settings into a single measure, expressing the overall computation costs. Using this metric, we show that the total space--time sampling volume required in a variational loop can be reduced dramatically from [MATH] to [MATH] for a hardware-efficient ansatz, allowing an exponential reduction in time and size of the quantum hardware. These results demonstrate that large, structured solid-state Hamiltonians can be simulated on substantially smaller quantum registers with controlled sampling overhead and manageable circuit complexity, extending the reach of variational quantum algorithms on near-term devices.

.
tldr: A logarithmic-qubit encoding for simulating single-particle Hamiltonians on near-term quantum devices, reducing qubit count and measurement settings exponentially.
motivation: Current quantum hardware has limited qubits and circuit depth, making simulation of large solid-state Hamiltonians challenging.
method: Maps N physical sites to log N qubits using a Gray-code-inspired measurement strategy and a compatible variational circuit.
result: The total space-time sampling volume is reduced from O(N^2) to O(log^2 N) for a hardware-efficient ansatz.
conclusion: Large structured Hamiltonians can be simulated on smaller quantum registers with controlled overhead, extending the reach of variational algorithms.

title: Quantum Optimal Control For Coherent Spin Dynamics Of Radical Pairs Via Pontryagin Maximum Principle
authors: Ugur G. Abdulla, Jose H. Rodrigues, And Jean-Jacques Slotine
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2096 (2026).

This paper aims to devise the shape of the external electromagnetic field that drives the spin dynamics of radical pairs to a quantum coherent state through maximization of the triplet-born singlet yield in biochemical reactions. The model is a Schrödinger system with spin Hamiltonians given by the sum of Zeeman interaction and hyperfine coupling interaction terms. We introduce a one-parameter family of optimal control problems by coupling the Schrödinger system to a control field through filtering equations for the electromagnetic field. Fréchet differentiability and the Pontryagin Maximum Principle in Hilbert space are proved, and the bang-bang structure of the optimal control is established. A new iterative Pontryagin Maximum Principle (IPMP) method for the identification of the bang-bang optimal control is developed. Numerical simulations based on IPMP and the gradient projection method (GPM) in Hilbert spaces are pursued, and the convergence, stability, and the regularization effect are demonstrated. Comparative analysis of filtering with regular optimal electromagnetic field versus non-filtering with bang-bang optimal field ([MATH][MATH]) demonstrates that the change of the maxima of the singlet yield is less than 1%. The results open a venue for a potential experimental work on magnetoreception as a manifestation of quantum biological phenomena.

.
tldr: Applies quantum optimal control to maximize singlet yield in radical pair spin dynamics, using Pontryagin's maximum principle.
motivation: To understand magnetoreception as a quantum biological phenomenon by controlling spin dynamics of radical pairs.
method: Formulates an optimal control problem for the Schrödinger equation with spin Hamiltonians, proves Fréchet differentiability and bang-bang structure via PMP, and develops an iterative PMP algorithm.
result: The optimal control is bang-bang; filtering with regular field vs. bang-bang field changes singlet yield by less than 1%.
conclusion: The method provides a way to design electromagnetic fields for coherent spin control, with potential applications in magnetoreception experiments.

title: Amplitude-dependent Quantum Hydrodynamics From A \(\coth\)-Madelung Ansatz
authors: C. Dedes
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06561v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate a nonlinear extension of the Madelung transformation based on a hyperbolic phase--amplitude coupling of the form \[ \Psi = R e^{\imath\theta \coth R}, \] where \(R\) is a real amplitude field and \(\theta\) is an auxiliary phase coordinate governed by Schr\"odinger's equation. In contrast to the conventional polar decomposition, this construction imposes a singular hyperbolic relation between amplitude and phase, thereby endowing the Bohmian or hydrodynamic description with an intrinsically geometric structure. We show that the associated velocity field acquires a density-gradient contribution, producing generalized continuity equations and modified quantum force terms. When interpreted as a complex macroscopic order parameter, this generalized phase structure leads to modified superconducting electrodynamics; in particular, the London equations acquire additional contributions that render the Meissner response sensitive to spatial density gradients. The proposed framework is motivated by broader developments involving complex group velocities, dissipative wave propagation, and amplitude-sensitive transport in quantum systems.
tldr: A nonlinear Madelung transformation with hyperbolic phase-amplitude coupling leads to modified quantum hydrodynamics and superconducting electrodynamics.
motivation: To explore a geometric extension of the Madelung transformation that introduces density-gradient contributions to the velocity field and quantum force.
method: The paper proposes a hyperbolic ansatz Ψ = R e^{iθ coth R} and derives generalized continuity equations and modified London equations from the Schrödinger equation.
result: The velocity field acquires a density-gradient term, and the London equations gain additional contributions making the Meissner response sensitive to spatial density gradients.
conclusion: The framework provides a new perspective on quantum hydrodynamics and may have implications for amplitude-sensitive transport in quantum systems.

This construction replaces the conventional polar decomposition with a singular hyperbolic relation between amplitude and phase, thereby endowing the Bohmian or hydrodynamic description with an intrinsically geometric structure. The authors show that the associated velocity field acquires a density-gradient contribution, leading to generalized continuity equations and modified quantum force terms. When interpreted as a complex macroscopic order parameter, this generalized phase structure modifies superconducting electrodynamics; in particular, the London equations gain additional contributions that make the Meissner response sensitive to spatial density gradients. The work is motivated by broader developments involving complex group velocities, dissipative wave propagation, and amplitude-sensitive transport in quantum systems.

Derives generalized continuity equations and modified quantum force terms due to density-gradient contributions in the velocity field.
Extends the framework to superconducting electrodynamics, showing that the London equations acquire additional terms that couple the Meissner response to spatial density gradients.
Provides a geometric reinterpretation of the Bohmian/hydrodynamic description of quantum mechanics.

The authors start by defining a new ansatz for the wavefunction Ψ = R e^{iθ coth R}, which introduces a hyperbolic coupling between amplitude R and phase θ. They then substitute this ansatz into the Schrödinger equation to derive modified hydrodynamic equations. The analysis involves computing the velocity field v = (ħ/m) ∇(θ coth R) and identifying additional terms proportional to ∇R. The authors also examine the implications for the quantum potential and force. For the superconducting application, they treat Ψ as a macroscopic order parameter and derive modified London equations by considering the current density j ∝ |Ψ|^2 v. The derivations are formal and rely on standard calculus and differential geometry, but no numerical simulations or experimental data are presented.

In the superconducting context, the London equations become ∇×j = -(n_s e^2/m) B + (eħ/m) ∇×(ρ ∇θ coth R) + additional gradient terms, indicating that the Meissner effect is no longer purely diamagnetic but depends on density gradients. No specific numerical values or quantitative predictions are provided; the results are expressed in general analytical forms.

The paper is clearly written and logically structured, making the derivations easy to follow.

However, the lack of empirical validation and the somewhat ad hoc nature of the hyperbolic coupling limit its immediate impact. The work is likely to be of interest to theorists working on nonlinear quantum mechanics, Bohmian mechanics, and unconventional superconductivity, but further development and experimental predictions are needed to establish its relevance.

title: Regular And Chaotic Dynamics Of Nonlinear Optomechanical Systems Controlled By Modulated Light
authors: A. P. Saiko, G. A. Rusetsky, S. A. Markevich, R. Fedaruk
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06997v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The nonlinear dynamics of a mechanical resonator in an optomechanical system with linear, quadratic and cubic photon-vibration interactions (with respect to mechanical displacements) in a modulated driving field under conditions of adiabatic elimination of the optical field is studied. Based on the constructed bifurcation diagrams of the mechanical coordinate and the largest Lyapunov exponent as a function of the modulation amplitude, as well as power spectra, phase portraits and Poincare sections, regions of regular and chaotic dynamics of the optomechanical system are identified. It is also shown that for a certain modulation amplitude in the presence of all three types of interactions, chaotic dynamics of the mechanical resonator (oscillator) is realized, which is replaced by quasi-periodic oscillations in the absence of cubic interaction, and the system returns to chaotic behavior if only linear interaction remains. This non-monotonic dependence of chaotic dynamics on the order of nonlinearity originates from the interplay between parametric driving and effective potential reshaping and manifests that nonlinearity does not always enhance chaos. For an optomechanical system in a membrane-in-the-middle configuration, where only quadratic photon-vibration interaction is present, it is demonstrated that at small modulation amplitudes the mechanical oscillator exhibits quasi-periodic motion in each of the wells of a symmetric two-minimum potential, whereas large modulation amplitudes lead to chaotic motion, involving interwell transitions.
tldr: This paper studies nonlinear dynamics and chaos in optomechanical systems with modulated driving, focusing on regular and chaotic motion of a mechanical resonator.
motivation: Understanding nonlinear dynamics in optomechanical systems is important for controlling mechanical resonators in quantum hybrid systems, but the paper is primarily classical and dynamical systems oriented.
method: Bifurcation diagrams, largest Lyapunov exponents, power spectra, phase portraits, and Poincaré sections are used to analyze the dynamics under linear, quadratic, and cubic photon-vibration interactions.
result: Chaotic dynamics depends non-monotonically on the order of nonlinearity; cubic interaction can suppress chaos, and in a membrane-in-the-middle configuration, large modulation amplitudes induce interwell chaotic motion.
conclusion: Nonlinearity does not always enhance chaos; the interplay of parametric driving and potential reshaping determines the onset of chaos.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates the nonlinear dynamics of a mechanical resonator in an optomechanical system that includes linear, quadratic, and cubic photon-vibration interactions, under a modulated driving field and with adiabatic elimination of the optical field. A key finding is that for a certain modulation amplitude, chaotic dynamics occur when all three interactions are present; removing the cubic interaction leads to quasi-periodic oscillations, while retaining only the linear interaction restores chaos. This non-monotonic dependence on nonlinearity order arises from the interplay between parametric driving and effective potential reshaping, demonstrating that nonlinearity does not always enhance chaos. Additionally, for a membrane-in-the-middle configuration with only quadratic interaction, small modulation amplitudes yield quasi-periodic motion in each well of a symmetric double-well potential, while large amplitudes induce chaotic motion with interwell transitions.

Identification of specific modulation amplitudes where chaos is suppressed by adding cubic interaction but restored when only linear interaction remains.

Use of bifurcation diagrams, Lyapunov exponents, power spectra, phase portraits, and Poincaré sections to comprehensively characterize the dynamics.

This is quantified by the largest Lyapunov exponent, which becomes positive in chaotic regimes. Relevance to experimental membrane-in-the-middle setups, offering testable predictions.

title: Quantum Correlations And Coherence In A Two-qubit Anisotropic $xy$ Under Magnetic Field
authors: Ahmed Jellal, Pablo D\'iaz, David Laroze
abstract: ArXiv:2606.07051v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study thermal quantum correlations and coherence in Heisenberg [MATH] model with anisotropic interactions under a uniform magnetic field [MATH]. Using concurrence [MATH], local quantum uncertainty (LQU), Bell-Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt (CHSH) nonlocality [MATH], and coherence [MATH] as quantifiers, we analyze how magnetic anisotropy [MATH], coupling anisotropy [MATH], Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya (DM) interaction [MATH], temperature [MATH], and magnetic field [MATH] modulate quantum resources. At low temperatures and relevant magnetic fields, the entanglement is maximized, but exhibits sudden death for [MATH], which turns into a smooth decay as [MATH] increases, highlighting its stabilizing role. LQU shows that stronger anisotropy suppresses quantum correlations, while [MATH] induces a non-monotonic response peaking at a critical field [MATH]. Bell-CHSH nonlocality violations ([MATH]) persist below [MATH], but thermal noise ([MATH]) suppresses them. Coherence [MATH] is most robust to thermal fluctuations, especially for high \( \delta_m \), which also dampens abrupt quantum phase transitions. The DM interaction is essential for entanglement generation, with [MATH] and anisotropy synergistically enhancing correlation resilience. We identify a hierarchy of thermal degradation: nonlocality ([MATH]) vanishes first, followed by entanglement ([MATH]), then general quantum correlations (LQU), while coherence [MATH] persists the longest. These results demonstrate tunable control of quantum resources via anisotropy and external parameters, providing insights for the design of robust spin-based quantum technologies.
tldr: This paper studies thermal quantum correlations and coherence in a two-qubit anisotropic XY model under a magnetic field, analyzing entanglement, nonlocality, and coherence as functions of anisotropy, DM interaction, temperature, and field.
motivation: To understand how magnetic anisotropy, coupling anisotropy, and Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction modulate quantum resources like entanglement and coherence in spin systems, which is relevant for designing robust quantum technologies.
method: The authors use concurrence, local quantum uncertainty (LQU), Bell-CHSH nonlocality, and coherence as quantifiers, and numerically compute these measures as functions of system parameters.
result: Entanglement exhibits sudden death at low anisotropy but smooth decay at higher anisotropy; LQU shows suppression by stronger anisotropy; Bell-CHSH violations persist only at low temperatures; coherence is most robust to thermal fluctuations.
conclusion: Tunable control of quantum resources is possible via anisotropy and external parameters, providing insights for spin-based quantum technologies.

At low temperatures and relevant magnetic fields, entanglement is maximized but exhibits sudden death for δ_m = 0, which transitions to a smooth decay as δ_m increases, indicating a stabilizing role of anisotropy. LQU shows that stronger anisotropy suppresses quantum correlations, while B induces a non-monotonic response peaking at a critical field B_c. Bell-CHSH nonlocality violations (B > 2) persist below B_c but are suppressed by thermal noise (T ≥ 1). Coherence C_l is most robust to thermal fluctuations, especially for high δ_m, which also dampens abrupt quantum phase transitions. The DM interaction is essential for entanglement generation, with D and anisotropy synergistically enhancing correlation resilience. The authors identify a hierarchy of thermal degradation: nonlocality vanishes first, followed by entanglement, then general quantum correlations (LQU), while coherence persists the longest. These results demonstrate tunable control of quantum resources via anisotropy and external parameters, providing insights for the design of robust spin-based quantum technologies.

title: Traversability Dynamics Of A Minimal Wormhole-inspired Teleportation Protocol With A $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric non-Hermitian Deformation
authors: Sudhanva Joshi And Sunil Kumar Mishra
abstract:
Author(s): Sudhanva Joshi and Sunil Kumar Mishra

Holography-inspired teleportation has recently emerged as a significant area of research in quantum many-body systems. In this work, we investigate the effects of [MATH]-symmetric nonunitary deformations on the traversability of the wormhole-inspired teleportation protocol modeled by coupled…


[Phys. Rev. A 113, 062419] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the effect of PT-symmetric non-Hermitian deformations on a holography-inspired teleportation protocol, finding that such deformations can enhance traversability.
motivation: To understand how non-unitary, PT-symmetric dynamics affect the traversability of wormhole-inspired teleportation in quantum many-body systems.
method: The authors model the teleportation protocol using coupled SYK-like systems and introduce a PT-symmetric non-Hermitian deformation, then analyze the out-of-time-order correlators and mutual information to quantify traversability.
result: The PT-symmetric deformation can enhance the traversability of the teleportation protocol, as measured by increased mutual information and improved signal transmission.
conclusion: Non-Hermitian deformations provide a new knob to control quantum teleportation in holographic settings, with potential implications for quantum information processing.

[Phys. Rev. A 113, 062609] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies how the Unruh effect affects the precision of estimating Gaussian channel parameters using quantum metrology.
motivation: Previous work on Gaussian channel estimation ignored relativistic effects; the Unruh effect introduces noise that may limit estimation precision.
method: The authors model a Gaussian channel in an accelerated frame, compute the quantum Fisher information for parameter estimation, and analyze the impact of acceleration.
result: The Unruh effect degrades estimation precision, but optimal measurements can partially mitigate the loss.
conclusion: Relativistic effects must be considered in quantum metrology for Gaussian channels, especially in high-acceleration scenarios.

title: Optimizing Doppler Laser Cooling Protocols For Quantum Sensing With Three-dimensional Ion Crystals In A Penning Trap

method: The authors develop an efficient numerical method to simulate and optimize Doppler laser cooling protocols for 3D ion crystals in a Penning trap.
result: They identify optimal cooling parameters that achieve lower temperatures and faster cooling times compared to standard protocols.
conclusion: The optimized cooling protocols enable practical use of large 3D ion crystals for quantum sensing applications.

[Phys. Rev. A 113, 063709] Published Thu Jun 04, 2026.
tldr: Theoretical study of slow-light-enhanced photon drag in a tunneling-coupled quantum-dot system.
motivation: To explore enhanced lateral and rotary photon drag effects using quantum coherence in a quantum-dot system.
method: Density-matrix formalism to derive susceptibility, group index, and phase index under weak-field conditions.
result: Analytical expressions for enhanced photon drag due to slow light and interdot tunneling.
conclusion: The proposed system can achieve significant photon drag enhancement, relevant for optical manipulation.

title: Localization And Scattering Of A Photon In Quasiperiodic Qubit Arrays

abstract:

We study the localization and scattering of a single photon in a waveguide coupled to qubit arrays with quasiperiodic spacings. [Phys. Rev. A 113, 063704] Published Wed Jun 03, 2026.
tldr: The paper studies localization and scattering of a single photon in waveguide-coupled qubit arrays with quasiperiodic spacings, revealing a continuum of long-lived subradiant states.
motivation: Understanding photon transport in disordered quantum systems is important for quantum information processing, but the focus here is on quasiperiodic order rather than quantum networking or thermodynamics.
method: The authors model a waveguide coupled to qubit arrays with quasiperiodic spacings and analyze the scattering properties and localization of single photons using analytical and numerical methods.
result: They find that as quasiperiodic strength increases, localized subradiant states with extremely long lifetimes form a continuum band around the resonant frequency, contrasting with the discrete bound states in periodic arrays.
conclusion: The work provides insights into photon localization in quasiperiodic qubit arrays, which may have implications for quantum memory or slow-light applications, but is not directly aligned with the user's core interests.

title: Cellular Automata In $d$ Dimensions And Ground States Of Spin Models In $(d+1)$ Dimensions
authors: Konstantinos Sfairopoulos, Luke Causer, Jamie F. Mair, And Juan P. Garrahan

We show how the trajectories of [MATH]-dimensional cellular automata (CA) can be used to systematically construct the ground states of [MATH]-dimensional classical spin models, and we characterize their quantum phase transition, when in the presence of a transverse magnetic field. For each of the 256 …


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 064112] Published Wed Jun 03, 2026.
tldr: This paper constructs ground states of (d+1)-dimensional classical spin models from trajectories of d-dimensional cellular automata and studies their quantum phase transitions.
motivation: To establish a systematic connection between cellular automata and classical spin models, and to characterize the quantum phase transition when a transverse field is added.
method: The authors use the trajectories of d-dimensional cellular automata to define ground states of (d+1)-dimensional classical spin models, then analyze the quantum phase transition via a transverse field.
result: They show that each of the 256 elementary cellular automata in 1D corresponds to a 2D classical spin model, and characterize the quantum phase transition in the presence of a transverse field.
conclusion: The work provides a new mapping between cellular automata and spin models, but the connection to information thermodynamics is indirect and the contribution is more about statistical mechanics and phase transitions.

title: Violation Of Local Equilibrium Thermodynamics In One-dimensional Hamiltonian-Potts Model
authors: Hitomi Endo And Michikazu Kobayashi

We investigate nonequilibrium phase coexistence associated with a first-order phase transition by numerically studying a one-dimensional Hamiltonian-Potts model with fractional spatial derivatives. The fractional derivative is introduced so as to reproduce the low-wave-number density of states of th…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 064109] Published Tue Jun 02, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies nonequilibrium phase coexistence in a one-dimensional Hamiltonian-Potts model with fractional spatial derivatives, finding violations of local equilibrium thermodynamics.
motivation: To understand nonequilibrium phase transitions and test the validity of local equilibrium assumptions in systems with long-range interactions.
method: Numerical simulation of a one-dimensional Hamiltonian-Potts model with fractional spatial derivatives to reproduce low-wave-number density of states.
result: The system exhibits violation of local equilibrium thermodynamics during first-order phase transitions.
conclusion: Fractional derivative models can capture nonequilibrium effects beyond local equilibrium, relevant for systems with long-range interactions.

tldr: The paper shows that hydrodynamic tails in classical spin systems are determined by dynamical critical exponent and equilibrium thermodynamic properties.
motivation: Understanding late-time dynamics and ergodicity in many-body systems is fundamental to statistical mechanics.
method: Analytical calculations and numerical simulations of autocorrelation functions in classical spin models.
result: The precise form of hydrodynamic tails depends on the dynamical critical exponent and thermodynamic susceptibility of the observable.
conclusion: Classical spin systems exhibit universal hydrodynamic behavior governed by equilibrium properties and critical exponents.

Nucleation in active and driven fluids often resembles equilibrium behavior, but a departure occurs when large-scale density fluctuations are strongly suppressed. tldr: This paper studies nucleation in active hyperuniform fluids, showing that droplet formation is governed by a nonequilibrium quasipotential rather than classical reversible work.
motivation: Understanding nucleation in active fluids is important for nonequilibrium statistical mechanics, but the paper focuses on a specific phenomenon (hyperuniformity) that is not central to the researcher's interests.
method: The authors theoretically analyze droplet nucleation in active fluids with suppressed density fluctuations, deriving a nonequilibrium quasipotential that replaces the classical reversible work.
result: They find that hyperuniformity reshapes nucleation and capillary-wave dynamics, leading to deviations from equilibrium behavior.
conclusion: The work provides insights into nonequilibrium phase transitions but does not directly address information thermodynamics or quantum systems.

result: They find that the large deviation functions exhibit singularities corresponding to dynamical phase transitions of trajectories.
conclusion: The work provides illustrative examples of dynamical phase transitions in nonergodic stochastic processes, contributing to the theory of large deviations.

The rotors are constrained to rotate in a plane about fixed pivot points and coupled by springs, such that in equilibrium, the neighboring rotors lie on opposite sides of the chain axis. The linearized limit of this model val…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 054141] Published Thu May 28, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies heat conduction in a 1D chain of rigid rotors, revealing a nonlinearity-induced transition from ballistic to diffusive transport in a topological metamaterial.
motivation: Understanding heat transport in nonlinear topological systems is important for thermal management and fundamental physics, but the paper focuses on classical nonlinear dynamics rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: The authors model a chain of coupled rotors with a topological linear spectrum and introduce nonlinearities, then compute heat current and conductivity using molecular dynamics simulations and analytical approximations.
result: They find that weak nonlinearity preserves ballistic transport, while strong nonlinearity leads to diffusive transport with a finite thermal conductivity, indicating a transition controlled by nonlinearity strength.
conclusion: The work demonstrates that nonlinearity can induce a transition in heat conduction in topological metamaterials, but the results are classical and not directly connected to quantum information or thermodynamics.

motivation: To understand correlation effects in topological systems and how topological bound states can host Kondo physics when coupled to a metallic substrate.

result: They demonstrate that the Kondo temperature can be tuned by the topological mass parameter, showing a crossover from Kondo to unscreened regimes.
conclusion: Topological bound states provide a controllable platform for Kondo physics, with potential applications in quantum simulation and sensing.

title: Imaginary Time Spectral Transforms For Excited-state Preparation

method: Combines a shift-invert spectral transformation with imaginary time evolution to avoid explicit matrix inversion, implemented via tensor-network simulations and compatible with hybrid quantum-classical platforms.
result: Demonstrates successful preparation of excited eigenstates in disordered spin chains, showing accuracy and efficiency compared to standard approaches.

title: Variational Processing Of Multimode Squeezed Light
